\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-scale text corpora are increasingly contaminated by synthetic content that has itself been generated from earlier synthetic content.
Each pass through a language model constitutes a lossy channel: first-generation synthetic text retains much of the information structure of its human-written source, but within just two or three generations the output is qualitatively different---tail modes vanish, lexical diversity contracts, and surprisal distributions flatten~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024model}.
This recursive degradation is not merely a theoretical concern; as synthetic text proliferates on the open web, training corpora inevitably ingest documents at varying generational depths, amplifying the risk of model collapse in downstream systems.
Yet the dominant paradigm in synthetic text detection treats all machine-generated text identically: a document is classified as human or synthetic, with no regard for how many rounds of recursive generation it has undergone.
This binary framing discards the generational depth dimension entirely.

The gap cuts across three research communities.
Binary detection methods---including DivEye~\cite{basani2026diveye}, Min-K\%++~\cite{zhang2024minkpp}, and CoDeC~\cite{zawalski2026codec}---achieve strong human-versus-machine separation but produce no depth estimate.
The model collapse literature provides macro-level characterizations of recursive degradation: Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} demonstrated irreversible tail loss, Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} proved convergence to a fixed point, and Schaeffer et al.~\cite{schaeffer2025position} organized the field into a taxonomy of eight definitions---yet none of these works provides a tool for estimating the generational depth of an individual text.
Data selection methods such as DSIR~\cite{xie2023dsir}, D4~\cite{tirumala2023d4}, and DoReMi~\cite{xie2023doremi} perform distribution matching to improve corpus quality but ignore recursive depth altogether.
The closest prior work is Drayson et al.~\cite{drayson2025}, who combined binary machine-generated text detection with stratified importance resampling to prevent model collapse---but their approach remains fundamentally binary.
No existing method estimates how many rounds of recursive generation a text has undergone, nor quantifies the boundary beyond which such estimation becomes infeasible.

Recursive generation forms an iterated lossy channel; the Data Processing Inequality guarantees that the original signal degrades monotonically across generations, motivating the existence of a finite discrimination boundary $\Kstar$ beyond which adjacent generations become indistinguishable.
Markov chain convergence further implies that adjacent-generation distributions converge to a shared stationary distribution, so the classifier's task grows harder with each step.
Motivated by this theoretical structure, we set out to empirically measure $\Kempirical$---the maximum depth at which a classifier can reliably distinguish adjacent generations.
Our approach combines a 15-dimensional statistical feature pipeline---capturing surprisal moments, surprisal derivatives, vocabulary diversity, and frequency tail statistics---with an Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) LightGBM classifier that respects the ordinal structure of depth.
We operationalize $\Kempirical$ as the deepest generation at which adjacent depths remain statistically distinguishable, with the bootstrap 95\% CI for pairwise $\auc$ exceeding an operational threshold $\theta = 0.60$ (formal definition in Section~\ref{sec:method}).
The choice of interpretable statistical features---rather than learned representations---is deliberate: it enables cross-generator transfer without retraining and permits attribution of discriminative power to specific text properties.

Our contributions are organized into two groups.
The primary contribution is a systematic empirical characterization of $\Kempirical$ and its properties:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
  \item \textbf{$\Kempirical = 2$: a consistent boundary across all tested conditions.}
    Across 4 model-mode configurations and 4 decoding strategies (8 conditions total), all 1v2 bootstrap CI lower bounds exceed $\theta = 0.60$ and all 2v3 CI upper bounds fall below $\theta$, with permutation $p \leq 0.002$ for all boundary comparisons.
    The most marginal case is Qwen-continuation, where $\text{CI}_\text{lower} = 0.6015$.
    $\Kempirical = 2$ is thus established as a consistent discrimination boundary across all 8 tested conditions at $\leq$1.5B scale, suggesting universality beyond the specific models and decoding strategies studied.
    Higher decoding entropy increases signal strength ($\auc_{1,2}$: $0.69$ greedy $\to$ $0.70$ at $T{=}1.2$) but does not shift the boundary.

  \item \textbf{Cross-model transfer.}
    Classifiers trained on one continuation-mode model and evaluated on another retain 80--92\% of within-model accuracy (Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo: 90--92\%).
    At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model $\auc$ exceeds 0.96 universally.
    Transfer retention of 80--92\% suggests a large text-intrinsic component of the depth signal, rather than generator-specific artifacts.

  \item \textbf{Degradation ordering consistency.}
    Single-feature $\auc$ rankings are highly correlated across continuation-mode models (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$), with the same top features---\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std}, \texttt{surp\_d2\_std}---appearing across all three families.
    This shared ordering suggests a common degradation mechanism: each generation step smooths the token-level surprisal landscape.
    A limitation is that depth-pair-level agreement weakens ($\tau \approx 0.37$ at 1v2), indicating that individual feature contributions at the boundary vary across models.

  \item \textbf{Generation mode analysis.}
    Within Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, rewrite mode yields 1v2 $\auc = 0.6955$ versus continuation's $0.6112$ ($\Delta = +8.4$\,pp), but rewrite-trained classifiers transfer poorly across models (61--63\% retention versus 80--92\% for continuation).
    Cross-mode transfer is asymmetric: continuation$\to$rewrite retains 89\% while rewrite$\to$continuation retains 82\%.
    Continuation mode is therefore recommended as the canonical condition for cross-model comparisons.
\end{enumerate}

\noindent As a secondary contribution, we investigate whether the coarse 3-class ordinal signal implied by $\Kempirical = 2$ enables \emph{graduated filtering}---depth-aware data curation that preserves mildly contaminated text (depth~1, retaining most original signal) while removing deeply corrupted text (depth~$\geq 3$)---and whether such filtering can improve upon binary approaches that discard all synthetic content indiscriminately (Section~\ref{sec:experiments}).

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section~\ref{sec:related_work} reviews related work.
Section~\ref{sec:method} describes the method.
Section~\ref{sec:experiments} presents experimental results.
Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses implications and limitations.
Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

3	
4	\paragraph{Model Collapse and Recursive Generation.}
5	Training on model-generated data can cause progressive distribution shift known as \emph{model collapse}.
6	Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} showed that iteratively training language models on their own outputs leads to irreversible tail-distribution degradation, with minority modes vanishing across generations.
7	Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} formalized this for self-consuming generative models, proving convergence to a fixed point under mild regularity conditions.
8	Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws for collapse, demonstrating that tail probability mass is lost at rates predictable from model and data scale.
9	Further work shows that even a vanishingly small fraction of synthetic data suffices to trigger collapse, with the effect amplified in larger models~\citep{dohmatob2025strong}.
10	Schaeffer et al.~\cite{schaeffer2025position} organized the fragmented literature into a taxonomy of eight definitions across three families.
11	Our $\Kstar$ aligns with their Family~B (distributional deformation), specifically D4 (collapsing variance) and D6 (mode entanglement)---the features that degrade most rapidly in our experiments are precisely variance-based surprisal measures.
12	Kazdan et al.~\cite{kazdan2025collapse} distinguished \emph{replace} and \emph{accumulate} regimes: in the replace regime each generation completely supplants its predecessor, producing faster collapse.
13	Our prompt-chain protocol operates in the replace regime, so $\Kempirical = 2$ is a conservative lower bound; the accumulate regime would yield slower degradation and higher $\Kstar$.
14	Shi et al.~\cite{shi2025generalization} identified a generalization-to-memorization transition in recursively trained models, providing cross-modal evidence that information loss is progressive.
15	Gerstgrasser et al.~\cite{gerstgrasser2024inevitable} proved that collapse is avoidable when sufficient original data is retained alongside synthetic samples, a condition that depth-aware curation can enforce by construction.
16	These works characterize the macro dynamics of collapse but do not provide tools for per-text generational depth estimation.
17	
18	\paragraph{Binary Synthetic Text Detection.}
19	Distinguishing machine-generated from human-written text is a well-studied binary classification problem.
20	Early statistical approaches such as GLTR~\cite{gehrmann2019gltr} visualized per-token likelihood ranks to help human annotators spot generated text, establishing that token-level distributional cues are informative for detection.
21	Zellers et al.~\cite{zellers2019grover} demonstrated that the generating model itself is an effective detector, while Ippolito et al.~\cite{ippolito2020detection} analyzed how detection difficulty scales with generation quality.
22	Recent zero-shot methods have narrowed the gap: Mitchell et al.~\cite{mitchell2023detectgpt} introduced DetectGPT, which uses probability curvature to detect machine-generated text without access to the generating model.
23	Fast-DetectGPT~\citep{bao2024fast} dramatically accelerates this approach via conditional probability curvature, achieving a 340$\times$ speedup with improved accuracy.
24	Hans et al.~\cite{hans2024binoculars} proposed Binoculars, which computes the cross-perplexity ratio between two closely related language models to achieve near-perfect detection without any training data.
25	DivEye~\cite{basani2026diveye} uses surprisal diversity features to detect synthetic text without generator-specific training data, and Min-K\%++~\cite{zhang2024minkpp} adapts membership inference techniques to flag model-generated passages via outlier token likelihoods.
26	CoDeC~\cite{zawalski2026codec} frames contamination detection as in-context learning, calibrating thresholds from few-shot exemplars.
27	
28	All these methods produce binary outputs and do not distinguish generational depth.
29	The connection to membership inference is instructive: Min-K\%++ and related approaches test whether a text appeared in training data---a related but distinct question from how many recursive generation steps it has undergone.
30	A further limitation is that binary detectors cannot separate beneficial recursive generation (e.g., self-refinement, where a model iteratively improves its own output) from harmful recursive contamination, creating systematic false positives when applied to curated synthetic data.
31	Binary features are designed for the human-vs.-synthetic boundary and are not expected to capture fine-grained depth differences, as the distributional shift between adjacent generations is orders of magnitude smaller than the shift between human and first-generation text.
32	
33	\paragraph{Ordinal Classification.}
34	Ordinal regression methods exploit the natural ordering among class labels to improve generalization over nominal classifiers.
35	Cao et al.~\cite{cao2020coral} introduced CORAL, which enforces rank consistency through weight sharing in the output layer, guaranteeing that predicted cumulative probabilities are monotonically non-increasing.
36	Ordinal approaches have been applied in NLP tasks such as sentiment intensity prediction and essay scoring, where adjacent categories share more semantic overlap than distant ones.
37	Generational depth exhibits the same ordinal structure: text at depth~$k$ is distributionally closer to depth~$k\!\pm\!1$ than to depth~$k\!\pm\!3$, because each recursive generation step introduces an incremental distributional shift rather than a discontinuous one.
38	Despite this natural fit, ordinal classification has not been applied to synthetic text depth estimation.
39	The idea of decomposing ordinal problems into a series of binary decisions dates to Frank \& Hall~\cite{frank2001ordinal}; our Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) head follows this principle by learning $K\!-\!1$ cumulative boundary classifiers, yielding monotonic depth predictions and stronger calibration than a flat softmax baseline.
40	
41	\paragraph{Probing Classifiers.}
42	Linear and shallow MLP probes have become a standard tool for analyzing what information is encoded in pretrained representations~\cite{alain2017understanding,conneau2018probing}.
43	Belinkov~\cite{belinkov2022probing} surveys the methodology and cautions that probe complexity must be controlled to ensure that performance reflects representational content rather than probe capacity.
44	Our neural probe experiment follows this protocol: a two-layer MLP on frozen Qwen2.5-1.5B embeddings, where the probe's limited capacity ensures that discriminability reflects depth information already present in the representations rather than learned de novo.
45	
46	\paragraph{Data Selection and Curation.}
47	Principled data selection methods improve training corpus quality through distribution matching and deduplication.
48	DSIR~\cite{xie2023dsir} selects pretraining data by importance resampling against a target distribution.
49	D4~\cite{tirumala2023d4} combines deduplication with diversification to reduce redundancy, and DoReMi~\cite{xie2023doremi} learns domain weights via a proxy model to optimize downstream performance.
50	These methods operate on distributional properties of the corpus but do not estimate whether individual documents have undergone recursive generation.
51	
52	The closest prior work is Drayson et al.~\cite{drayson2025}, who combined binary machine-generated text detection with stratified importance resampling (SIR) to filter synthetic content and prevent model collapse.
53	Their approach is a special case of our graduated filtering framework: when $\Kstar = 1$, ordinal depth estimation reduces to binary classification, and depth-aware curation degenerates to their SIR-based scheme.
54	We generalize this binary formulation to ordinal depth estimation, enabling finer-grained curation that preserves mildly contaminated text (depth~1, retaining most original signal) while removing deeply corrupted text (depth~$\geq 3$).
55	Recent work demonstrates that external verification can prevent model collapse during recursive training~\citep{feng2025beyond}, positioning depth estimation as a natural verification signal for data curation.
56	Amin et al.~\cite{amin2025escaping} demonstrated that even weak quality signals suffice to escape model collapse when applied iteratively, suggesting that approximate depth estimates beyond $\Kempirical$ may remain practically useful.
57	Gambetta et al.~\cite{gambetta2025surplexity} proposed surplexity as a text quality metric correlated with generative degradation, though without explicit depth calibration.
58	
59	\paragraph{Watermarking and Provenance.}
60	An alternative approach embeds identifiers at generation time.
61	Kirchenbauer et al.~\cite{kirchenbauer2023watermark} proposed statistical watermarking for LLM outputs by partitioning the vocabulary into green and red token lists conditioned on preceding context.
62	Watermarking is complementary to depth estimation: it requires control over the generation process and cooperation from providers, whereas our method operates post-hoc on unwatermarked text.
63	The two approaches address different threat models---watermarking assumes a cooperative generator, while depth estimation targets uncontrolled settings where provenance metadata is unavailable.

15	Recursive text generation naturally forms an iterated lossy channel.
16	Let $X$ denote an original human-written document drawn from a source distribution $\mathcal{D}$.
17	A generation operator $G_\delta = \text{LLM} + \delta$, parameterized by a decoding strategy $\delta$ (e.g., nucleus sampling with top-$p$ and temperature $T$), produces successive generations:
18	\begin{equation}
19	  X \to Y_1 \to Y_2 \to \cdots \to Y_K, \quad Y_k = G_\delta(Y_{k-1}),
20	  \label{eq:markov}
21	\end{equation}
22	where $Y_0 \triangleq X$.
23	The sequence $\{Y_k\}_{k=0}^K$ forms a Markov chain, since each generation depends only on its immediate predecessor.
24	
25	By the Data Processing Inequality (DPI), mutual information between the original document and successive generations is monotonically non-increasing:
26	\begin{equation}
27	  I(X; Y_1) \geq I(X; Y_2) \geq \cdots \geq 0.
28	  \label{eq:dpi}
29	\end{equation}
30	Since mutual information is bounded below by zero, this monotone sequence converges: the original signal degrades monotonically across generations.
31	Moreover, when the generation operator defines a finite-state Markov chain, the marginal distributions of adjacent generations converge to a shared stationary distribution, so that any classifier's ability to distinguish depth $k$ from depth $k{+}1$ must eventually degrade to chance.
32	Together, these arguments guarantee the existence of a finite $\Ktheory$ beyond which adjacent generations are indistinguishable---the \emph{information-theoretic discrimination boundary}.
33	
34	Motivated by this theoretical guarantee, we set out to \emph{empirically measure} the discrimination boundary.
35	We define an operational lower bound $\Kempirical$ via a classifier's ability to distinguish adjacent generations:
36	\begin{equation}
37	  \Kempirical = \max\{k : \text{CI}_{\text{lower}}^{95\%}(\auc_{k,k+1}) > \theta\},
38	  \label{eq:kstar}
39	\end{equation}
40	where $\auc_{k,k+1}$ is the pairwise area under the ROC curve for distinguishing depth $k$ from $k{+}1$, $\text{CI}_{\text{lower}}^{95\%}$ denotes the lower bound of a bootstrap 95\% confidence interval (1{,}000 resamples), and $\theta$ is an operational threshold justified in \S\ref{sec:kstar_operational}.
41	Since any specific classifier can only recover a subset of the information-theoretically available signal, $\Kempirical \leq \Ktheory$ by construction.

90	\subsection{Ordinal Binary Decomposition Classifier}
91	\label{sec:classifier}
92	
93	Generational depth is inherently ordinal: depth~1 is closer to depth~0 than depth~3 is.
94	We exploit this structure via \emph{Ordinal Binary Decomposition} (OBD), which decomposes a $(K{+}1)$-class ordinal classification problem into $K$ cumulative binary sub-classifiers.
95	The $k$-th sub-classifier estimates the exceedance probability:
96	\begin{equation}
97	  P(\text{depth} > k \mid \mathbf{x}), \quad k = 0, 1, \ldots, K{-}1,
98	\end{equation}
99	where $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{15}$ is the feature vector.
100	Each sub-classifier is an independent LightGBM model (hyperparameters in Table~\ref{tab:s6_lgbm_params}).
101	Class probabilities are recovered via the decomposition $P(Y{=}0) = 1 - P(Y{>}0)$ and $P(Y{=}k) = P(Y{>}k{-}1) - P(Y{>}k)$ for $k \geq 1$.
102	The predicted depth is:
103	\begin{equation}
104	  \hat{d}(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{k} \; P(Y{=}k \mid \mathbf{x}).
105	\end{equation}
106	
107	We compared OBD-LightGBM against two alternatives: standard (unordered) multiclass LightGBM and ordinal logistic regression (LogisticAT).
108	OBD-LightGBM achieves lower mean absolute error (MAE) than multiclass LightGBM across all three model families (Qwen-rewrite: 0.984 vs.\ 1.016; Pythia: 1.107 vs.\ 1.140; OLMo: 1.147 vs.\ 1.181).
109	Ordinal logistic regression yields the lowest MAE overall (e.g., 0.911 on Qwen-rewrite) but at the cost of substantially degraded pairwise discrimination: mean pairwise $\auc$ of 0.4883 versus 0.6095 for OBD-LightGBM, averaged across the three families.
110	The low MAE of ordinal logistic regression stems from collapsing predictions toward central depths rather than improved discrimination---a pathology that renders it unsuitable when pairwise depth discriminability is the primary objective.

112	\subsection{Operationalizing $\Kstar$}
113	\label{sec:kstar_operational}
114	
115	We set the operational threshold at $\theta = 0.60$.
116	This choice is grounded in the permutation test null distribution: across all model configurations, the 95th percentile of the null $\auc$ (obtained from 500 random label permutations) falls below 0.55.
117	A threshold of $\theta = 0.60$ therefore requires classification performance that is statistically significantly above chance at the $\alpha = 0.05$ level.
118	
119	Uncertainty is quantified via bootstrap resampling (1{,}000 resamples) of $\auc_{k,k+1}$ for each adjacent depth pair.
120	$\Kempirical$ is defined as the maximum depth $k$ for which $\text{CI}_{\text{lower}}^{95\%}(\auc_{k,k+1}) > \theta$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:kstar}).
121	
122	We examine threshold sensitivity at $\theta \in \{0.55, 0.60, 0.65, 0.70\}$.
123	At $\theta = 0.60$, $\Kempirical = 2$ holds across all four model configurations, with all permutation $p$-values for depth pair $1$ vs.\ $2$ at $p = 0.002$.
124	At the more lenient $\theta = 0.55$, $\Kempirical = 3$ uniformly across all four configurations.
125	At the stricter $\theta = 0.65$, only the rewrite configuration retains $\Kempirical = 2$; continuation-mode configurations yield $\Kempirical = 1$.
126	At $\theta = 0.70$, $\Kempirical = 1$ universally.
127	This sensitivity profile confirms that $\Kempirical = 2$ is robust at our chosen threshold while remaining appropriately responsive to more stringent criteria.

167	\subsection{Generation Mode Control}
168	\label{sec:generation_mode_method}
169	
170	We investigate two generation modes that capture distinct recursive contamination scenarios:
171	
172	\paragraph{Continuation.}
173	The seed document is truncated to its first 128 tokens, and the LLM generates a continuation to 256 tokens.
174	This simulates scenarios where partial human text is extended by a model, a common pattern in collaborative writing and web content generation.
175	
176	\paragraph{Rewrite.}
177	The LLM receives the instruction ``Rewrite the following text while preserving its meaning'' and generates a full paraphrase.
178	This simulates content rewriting pipelines where existing text is rephrased at scale.
179	
180	We designate continuation as the \emph{canonical condition} for cross-model comparisons, based on three empirical findings from the cross-model transfer analysis.
181	First, classifiers trained on continuation-mode data retain 80--92\% accuracy when transferred across model families, versus only 61--63\% for rewrite-mode classifiers.
182	Second, the higher pairwise $\auc$ observed in rewrite mode ($\auc_{1,2} = 0.6955$ vs.\ $0.6112$ for continuation on Qwen) reflects instruction-following style artifacts rather than a stronger intrinsic depth signal, as evidenced by the poor cross-model transfer.
183	Third, the asymmetric transfer---continuation${\to}$rewrite retains 89\% performance versus rewrite${\to}$continuation at 82\%---indicates that continuation-mode features form a generalizable subset of what rewrite-mode classifiers exploit.
184	We therefore report continuation-mode results as primary and treat rewrite-mode results as an upper-bound ablation that quantifies the effect of mode-specific signal amplification.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

We evaluate generational depth estimation on four model configurations:
Pythia-1.4B and OLMo-1B in continuation mode, and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct in both rewrite and continuation modes.
All experiments use the OBD-LightGBM classifier with the 15-dimensional feature set described in Section~\ref{sec:method}.
Each configuration uses a balanced corpus of 5{,}000 texts per depth level (generations 0--5).
We organize results around four questions:
(1)~Does $\Kempirical = 2$ hold across configurations?
(2)~Do depth classifiers transfer across models?
(3)~Is the feature degradation ordering model-independent?
(4)~How does generation mode affect detectability?

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{$\Kempirical = 2$ Across All Configurations}
\label{sec:kstar_boundary}

Table~\ref{tab:kstar_ci} reports pairwise $\auc$ for adjacent depth pairs
across all four configurations, with bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals
(1{,}000 resamples) and permutation-test $p$-values for the critical 1v2
and 2v3 boundaries.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ for adjacent depth pairs.  Bootstrap 95\% CIs
and permutation $p$-values shown for the $\Kstar$ boundary rows (1v2,
2v3).  $\Kempirical = 2$ requires 1v2 $\text{CI}_\text{low} > \theta$
and 2v3 $\text{CI}_\text{high} < \theta$ with $\theta = 0.60$.
All 0v1 permutation $p \leq 0.002$ (Qwen-continuation 0v1: CI [0.9963, 0.9978], $p = 0.002$).}
\label{tab:kstar_ci}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
 & Qwen-rw & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-cont \\
\midrule
0v1 & 0.9956 & 0.9932 & 0.9970 & 0.9971 \\[4pt]
1v2 & 0.6955 & 0.6539 & 0.6145 & 0.6112 \\
{\footnotesize CI}
  & {\footnotesize [.6859,\,.7041]}
  & {\footnotesize [.6454,\,.6630]}
  & {\footnotesize [.6045,\,.6247]}
  & {\footnotesize [.6015,\,.6213]} \\
{\footnotesize $p$}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002} \\[4pt]
2v3 & 0.5893 & 0.5514 & 0.5496 & 0.5609 \\
{\footnotesize CI}
  & {\footnotesize [.5795,\,.5991]}
  & {\footnotesize [.5417,\,.5628]}
  & {\footnotesize [.5399,\,.5596]}
  & {\footnotesize [.5511,\,.5712]} \\
{\footnotesize $p$}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002} \\[4pt]
3v4 & 0.5435 & 0.5152 & 0.5091 & 0.5409 \\
4v5 & 0.5340 & 0.5136 & 0.5045 & 0.5141 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The pattern is uniform across all four configurations:
0v1 discrimination is near-perfect ($\auc > 0.99$),
followed by a sharp drop at 1v2 ($\auc$ range: 0.6112--0.6955),
with 2v3 falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$
($\auc$ range: 0.5496--0.5893).
All subsequent pairs (3v4, 4v5) converge toward chance.
Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay} visualizes this decay.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_auc_decay.pdf}
\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ as a function of depth pair across four model-mode configurations (solid) and four decoding strategies (dashed).  All configurations show a sharp drop between 0v1 and 1v2, with 2v3 and deeper pairs falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$ (horizontal dashed line).  Error bars show bootstrap 95\% CIs for model-mode configurations; decoding strategy curves omit CIs as they were computed on a separate experimental setup.}
\label{fig:auc_decay}
\end{figure}

For the $\Kempirical$ determination, all four 1v2 CI lower bounds exceed
$\theta$: Qwen-rewrite ($\text{CI}_\text{low} = 0.6859$), Pythia (0.6454),
OLMo (0.6045), and Qwen-continuation (0.6015).
Conversely, all four 2v3 CI upper bounds fall below $\theta$:
Qwen-rewrite ($\text{CI}_\text{high} = 0.5991$), Qwen-continuation (0.5712),
Pythia (0.5628), and OLMo (0.5596).
Permutation tests confirm $p = 0.002$ for all eight boundary comparisons.
Together these establish $\Kempirical = 2$ as a consistent discrimination boundary across all tested configurations at $\leq$1.5B scale, suggesting universality beyond the specific models studied.

The most marginal case is Qwen-continuation, where the 1v2 CI lower bound
(0.6015) exceeds $\theta$ by only 0.0015.  This narrow margin
indicates that $\Kempirical = 2$ is robust but not trivially so---continuation-mode
generation produces weaker depth artifacts than rewrite mode, pushing the
boundary closer to the detection threshold.

The absolute 1v2 $\auc$ varies across models:
Qwen-rewrite (0.6955) $>$ Pythia (0.6539) $>$ OLMo (0.6145) $\approx$ Qwen-continuation (0.6112).
Notably, the spread due to generation mode within a single model
(Qwen-rewrite vs.\ Qwen-continuation: $\Delta = 8.4$\,pp) exceeds the spread
across models in the same mode
(Pythia vs.\ OLMo: $\Delta = 3.9$\,pp),
suggesting that generation protocol is a stronger determinant
of detectability than model identity.
We examine both factors in Sections~\ref{sec:transfer}
and~\ref{sec:generation_mode}.

Beyond the $\Kempirical$ boundary, depth discrimination deteriorates
rapidly.
OLMo shows nonsignificant permutation $p$-values at 3v4
($p = 0.064$) and 4v5 ($p = 0.232$), indicating that depth
classification beyond generation~2 is indistinguishable from
random for this model.
Pythia retains marginal effects at these depths
($p = 0.006$ and $p = 0.008$, respectively),
while Qwen-continuation shows weak but detectable discrimination through
3v4 ($p = 0.002$) that fades at 4v5 ($p = 0.006$).

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{Cross-Model Transfer}
\label{sec:transfer}

Having established $\Kempirical = 2$ consistently, we next ask: is this boundary a property of the text itself, or an artifact of model self-familiarity?
To answer this, we train classifiers on one model's outputs and evaluate on another's.
Table~\ref{tab:transfer_matrix} shows the full
$4 \times 4$ transfer accuracy matrix for 6-class ordinal depth
classification.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Cross-model transfer accuracy (6-class ordinal
classification).  Diagonal entries (bold): within-model accuracy.
Off-diagonal: cross-model transfer.  Retention is computed as
off-diagonal accuracy divided by the diagonal entry of the training
model.}
\label{tab:transfer_matrix}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
Train $\downarrow$ / Test $\rightarrow$
  & Qwen-rw & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-cont \\
\midrule
Qwen-rw
  & \textbf{0.4229} & 0.2590 & 0.2653 & 0.3466 \\
Pythia
  & 0.2718 & \textbf{0.3856} & 0.3531 & 0.3287 \\
OLMo
  & 0.2768 & 0.3450 & \textbf{0.3822} & 0.3244 \\
Qwen-cont
  & 0.3440 & 0.3284 & 0.3112 & \textbf{0.3875} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\columnwidth]{figures/fig3_transfer_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{Cross-model transfer heatmap (6-class ordinal accuracy).
Rows: training model; columns: test model.
Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (both continuation mode) shows high
mutual transfer (90--92\% accuracy retention), while Qwen-rewrite
transfers poorly to continuation-mode models (61--63\%).
Diagonal entries are within-model baselines.}
\label{fig:transfer_heatmap}
\end{figure}

Two principal findings emerge (Figure~\ref{fig:transfer_heatmap}).
First, transfer between continuation-mode models is high.
Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo mutual transfer retains 90--92\% of within-model accuracy
(85--86\% retention by Kendall $\tau$).
The accuracy-based retention of 90--92\% is complemented by the
$\tau$-based retention of 85--86\%, indicating that not only
classification accuracy but also the relative depth ordering of
predictions is largely preserved.
Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$Pythia also transfers well
(84--85\% accuracy retention),
and Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$OLMo achieves 80--85\%.
These retention rates---80--92\% of within-model accuracy preserved across continuation-mode pairs---suggest that a large component of the depth signal is text-intrinsic rather than tied to a specific generator.

Second, Qwen-rewrite exhibits catastrophic transfer failure.
Classifiers trained on Qwen-rewrite retain only 61--63\% of
within-model accuracy when evaluated on Pythia or OLMo
(45--50\% by $\tau$).
The reverse direction transfers asymmetrically: Pythia/OLMo${\to}$Qwen-rewrite retains 70--72\% of within-model accuracy, higher than the forward 61--63\% but still far below continuation-mode transfer rates (80--92\%).
This confirms that rewrite-mode classifiers rely on generation
artifacts that do not generalize across models, in contrast
to Qwen-continuation, which achieves 80--85\% retention to the same targets.

At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model pairwise $\auc$ exceeds 0.96
for all model pairs, confirming that the human-vs.-synthetic
distinction is universally transferable regardless of generator
or mode.
The transfer degradation concentrates at deeper boundaries
(1v2 and beyond), where model- and mode-specific factors dominate.

The aggregate picture is one of modest cross-model loss:
mean pairwise $\auc$ is 0.6099 within-model versus 0.5905
cross-model.
This gap is driven primarily by Qwen-rewrite; among
continuation-mode pairs the within/cross difference narrows
further.

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{Feature Degradation Ordering}
\label{sec:feature_degradation}

The transfer results indicate that depth signals are largely text-intrinsic.
We next ask what drives discrimination: if the signal is text-intrinsic, different generators should rely on the same features in the same order.
We test this by computing single-feature $\auc$ rankings
independently for each model and comparing them via rank
correlation.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Top-3 features by single-feature $\auc$ ranking for each
model configuration.
Features shared across all three continuation-mode models are in bold.
Qwen-rewrite's top feature (\texttt{freq\_entropy}) is mode-specific.
Spearman $\rho$ (continuation-mode pairs): Pythia--OLMo 0.95,
Pythia--Qwen-continuation 0.9143, OLMo--Qwen-continuation 0.85.}
\label{tab:top_features}
\begin{tabular}{cllll}
\toprule
Rank & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-rw & Qwen-cont \\
\midrule
1
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
  & \texttt{freq\_entropy}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}} \\
2
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}} \\
3
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Among continuation-mode models, single-feature $\auc$ rankings
are highly correlated:
Pythia vs.\ OLMo $\rho = 0.95$,
Pythia vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\rho = 0.9143$,
OLMo vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\rho = 0.85$
(all $\rho \geq 0.85$).
The top-3 features---\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std},
and \texttt{surp\_d2\_std}---are shared (up to ordering) across
all three continuation-mode configurations
(Table~\ref{tab:top_features}).
All three measure variability of surprisal or its derivatives,
capturing the \emph{heterogeneity} of token-level predictability
across the text.
That these features degrade in a shared order across generators
suggests a common mechanism: each generation step smooths the
token-level surprisal landscape, reducing its variance in a
model-independent fashion.

Qwen-rewrite diverges: its top-ranked feature is
\texttt{freq\_entropy}, a lexical diversity measure absent from
the continuation-mode top-3 for any model.
This corroborates the transfer results in
Section~\ref{sec:transfer}---rewrite-mode classifiers learn
partly from instruction-following artifacts rather than the
shared surprisal-based signals.

Kendall $\tau$ provides a complementary, more conservative
perspective:
Pythia vs.\ OLMo $\tau = 0.733$,
Pythia vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\tau = 0.695$,
OLMo vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\tau = 0.543$.
Cross-mode correlations are lower:
Pythia vs.\ Qwen-rewrite $\tau = 0.467$,
OLMo vs.\ Qwen-rewrite $\tau = 0.429$.

\paragraph{Limitation.}
The high Spearman $\rho$ characterizes the \emph{aggregate}
feature ranking, but at the depth-pair level the agreement
weakens: $\tau \approx 0.37$ at the 1v2 boundary.
This means that while the overall importance ordering is shared,
the relative contribution of individual features at the
discrimination boundary---where precision matters most---varies
across models.
We view this as a genuine limitation of the text-intrinsic
interpretation and a direction for future investigation.

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{Generation Mode Effect}
\label{sec:generation_mode}

Finally, we ask whether generation mode---an experimental design choice rather than a text property---affects depth detectability.
Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct provides a controlled comparison: rewrite (instruction-based paraphrasing) and continuation (prompt truncation) share the same model weights, as defined in Section~\ref{sec:method}, isolating the effect of generation protocol.

Rewrite mode yields higher 1v2 $\auc$ than continuation:
0.6955 vs.\ 0.6112, a difference of $+$8.4 percentage points.
The advantage persists at 2v3
(0.5893 vs.\ 0.5609, $\Delta = +$2.8\,pp)
and narrows at 3v4
(0.5435 vs.\ 0.5409, $\Delta = +$0.3\,pp),
with both modes converging toward chance at deeper levels.
The amplified detectability under rewrite mode is consistent
with instruction-following introducing systematic deviations
from the source text's style---additional artifacts that are
discriminable but mode-specific rather than text-intrinsic.

Transfer between modes is asymmetric.
A classifier trained on Qwen-continuation and evaluated on Qwen-rewrite
retains 89\% of within-model accuracy
(0.3440 vs.\ 0.3875 diagonal),
whereas the reverse direction---Qwen-rewrite trained,
Qwen-continuation tested---retains 82\%
(0.3466 vs.\ 0.4229 diagonal).
The direction of the asymmetry is intuitive:
continuation-mode signals form a subset of the information
available in rewrite-mode data
(which adds instruction-following artifacts on top),
so a continuation-trained classifier can partially recognize
rewrite-mode outputs but not vice versa.

This asymmetry is mirrored in the feature rankings.
Qwen-rewrite's top feature (\texttt{freq\_entropy}) is
mode-specific and ranks outside the top-3 for every
continuation-mode model.
Qwen-continuation's top feature (\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}) is shared
with Pythia and OLMo, confirming that continuation mode
captures primarily text-intrinsic depth signals.

The practical implication is a detectability--generalizability
tradeoff.
Rewrite-mode classifiers achieve higher absolute $\auc$ but
transfer poorly across models
(Qwen-rewrite$\to$Pythia/OLMo: 61--63\% retention).
Continuation-mode classifiers sacrifice 8.4\,pp of within-model
$\auc$ but achieve robust cross-model transfer
(Qwen-continuation$\to$Pythia: 84--85\%).
For deployment scenarios requiring model-agnostic depth
estimation, continuation-mode features provide a more reliable
foundation despite lower raw discriminability.

2	\label{sec:graduated-filtering}
3	
4	The $\Kempirical = 2$ boundary establishes a three-tier taxonomy: human (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$).
5	Binary filtering discards all synthetic content indiscriminately, sacrificing depth-1 text that retains most of the original signal.
6	We ask whether exploiting the coarse ordinal structure---weighting samples by predicted depth rather than applying a hard human/synthetic threshold---improves downstream language model quality.

8	\paragraph{Filtering strategies.}
9	We compare six data curation strategies applied to a corpus of 30{,}000 documents (5{,}000 per depth level, depths 0--5) produced by the generational depth pipeline:
10	
11	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
12	  \item \textbf{No-filter}: all documents receive uniform weight (baseline).
13	
14	  \item \textbf{Binary-ours}: a LightGBM classifier trained on the 15-dimensional feature set distinguishes human (depth~0) from synthetic (depth~$\geq 1$).
15	  Each document receives weight $w = 1 - P(\text{synthetic})$.
16	  This represents the natural binary extension of our depth estimation framework.
17	
18	  \item \textbf{Binary-Drayson}: stratified importance resampling following Drayson et al.~\cite{drayson2025}, with $w_j = (1 - q(x_j))^b / Z$, $b = 1.5$, and oversampling factor $k = 1.5$.
19	  This is the strongest existing baseline for contamination-aware data curation.
20	
21	  \item \textbf{Graduated}: our proposed depth-aware strategy.
22	  The OBD-LightGBM classifier (Section~\ref{sec:classifier}) predicts a full depth distribution $P(d \mid \mathbf{x})$ for each document, from which we compute the expected depth $\hat{d} = \sum_d d \cdot P(d \mid \mathbf{x})$.
23	  Sample weights follow an exponential decay: $w = \exp(-\alpha \cdot \hat{d})$, where $\alpha$ controls the penalty for predicted depth.

\subsection{Graduated Filtering for Depth-Aware Data Curation}
\label{sec:graduated-filtering}

The $\Kempirical = 2$ boundary establishes a three-tier taxonomy: human (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$).
Binary filtering discards all synthetic content indiscriminately, sacrificing depth-1 text that retains most of the original signal.
We ask whether exploiting the coarse ordinal structure---weighting samples by predicted depth rather than applying a hard human/synthetic threshold---improves downstream language model quality.

\paragraph{Filtering strategies.}
We compare six data curation strategies applied to a corpus of 30{,}000 documents (5{,}000 per depth level, depths 0--5) produced by the generational depth pipeline:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
  \item \textbf{No-filter}: all documents receive uniform weight (baseline).

  \item \textbf{Binary-ours}: a LightGBM classifier trained on the 15-dimensional feature set distinguishes human (depth~0) from synthetic (depth~$\geq 1$).
  Each document receives weight $w = 1 - P(\text{synthetic})$.
  This represents the natural binary extension of our depth estimation framework.

  \item \textbf{Binary-Drayson}: stratified importance resampling following Drayson et al.~\cite{drayson2025}, with $w_j = (1 - q(x_j))^b / Z$, $b = 1.5$, and oversampling factor $k = 1.5$.
  This is the strongest existing baseline for contamination-aware data curation.

  \item \textbf{Graduated}: our proposed depth-aware strategy.
  The OBD-LightGBM classifier (Section~\ref{sec:classifier}) predicts a full depth distribution $P(d \mid \mathbf{x})$ for each document, from which we compute the expected depth $\hat{d} = \sum_d d \cdot P(d \mid \mathbf{x})$.
  Sample weights follow an exponential decay: $w = \exp(-\alpha \cdot \hat{d})$, where $\alpha$ controls the penalty for predicted depth.
  Low $\alpha$ values retain more synthetic content with gentle down-weighting; high $\alpha$ values approximate hard filtering.
  We sweep $\alpha \in \{0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9\}$.

  \item \textbf{Surprisal}: a feature-based heuristic that retains documents whose mean surprisal exceeds the corpus median, exploiting the observation that deeper generations exhibit lower surprisal variance (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}).

  \item \textbf{DSIR}: Data Selection via Importance Resampling~\cite{xie2023dsir}, using bigram feature hashing with the depth-0 subcorpus as the reference distribution.
  This represents the state-of-the-art domain-matching baseline that is agnostic to generational depth.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Training setup.}
We fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct via LoRA (rank~8, $\alpha_{\text{LoRA}} = 16$, target modules: \texttt{q\_proj}, \texttt{v\_proj}, dropout 0.05) on the filtered corpus for 3 epochs with learning rate $2 \times 10^{-5}$, batch size 4 with gradient accumulation 8, warmup ratio 0.1, and bfloat16 precision.
Documents are truncated to 512 tokens.
For strategies that produce continuous weights (graduated, binary-ours, binary-Drayson, DSIR), zero-weight samples are removed and the remaining samples are drawn via weighted random sampling; for binary strategies (surprisal), excluded samples are dropped outright.
Each strategy is evaluated across 5 random seeds (42, 123, 456, 789, 1024); the graduated strategy is further crossed with 5 $\alpha$ values, yielding 25 additional runs.
A base model baseline (no fine-tuning) is included for reference.
The total experimental budget is approximately 50 runs.

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We evaluate on two standard benchmarks via lm-eval-harness: MMLU (14{,}042 test examples, 0-shot) and HellaSwag (10{,}042 validation examples, 0-shot).
We report mean accuracy $\pm$ standard deviation across seeds.

1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\subsection{Theoretical Implications of $\Kempirical = 2$}
5	\label{sec:discuss_kstar}
6	
7	The Data Processing Inequality guarantees the existence of a finite $\Ktheory$ beyond which adjacent generations become indistinguishable (Section~\ref{sec:formulation}).
8	Our empirical result---$\Kempirical = 2$ consistently across all 8 tested configurations (4 model-mode combinations and 4 decoding strategies; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}, Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay})---establishes that this boundary is not only finite but remarkably shallow at the $\leq$1.5B parameter scale.
9	
10	The shallowness of $\Kempirical$ is explained by the rate of information loss across generations.
11	The 0v1 boundary is near-trivially separable ($\auc > 0.99$ across all configurations; Table~\ref{tab:kstar_ci}), reflecting the large distributional gap between human text and first-generation synthetic text.
12	At the 1v2 boundary, $\auc$ drops by approximately 30 percentage points ($\auc$ range: 0.6112--0.7039 across all eight model$\times$decoding conditions; Table~\ref{tab:kstar_ci}, Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay}; see also Figure~\ref{fig:s1_auc_decay_ci} in the Appendix), indicating that the majority of the discriminative signal is consumed in the first generation step.
13	By the 2v3 boundary, $\auc$ falls to 0.5496--0.5917 across all eight model$\times$decoding conditions (upper bound from nucleus $p{=}0.9$ decoding; Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay})---below the operational threshold $\theta = 0.60$---and deeper pairs converge toward chance.
14	Recursive generation thus acts as a severely lossy channel whose information bottleneck is traversed within two steps.
15	
16	The feature degradation analysis (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}) provides mechanistic evidence for this rapid collapse.
17	The most discriminative features---surprisal variance (\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std}) and its derivatives---all capture the heterogeneity of token-level predictability.
18	Human text exhibits high surprisal variance reflecting diverse syntactic structures and unpredictable discourse patterns.
19	The first generation step smooths this variance substantially, replacing high-surprisal tokens and atypical constructions with more predictable alternatives; the second step reduces the remaining variance to near-floor levels, leaving insufficient statistical fingerprint for reliable adjacent-depth discrimination.
20	Crucially, this degradation ordering is consistent across model families (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$ for all continuation-mode pairs; Table~\ref{tab:top_features}), suggesting that the two-step information loss is governed by the autoregressive generation mechanism itself rather than by model-specific biases.
21	
22	This pattern aligns with findings from the model collapse literature.
23	Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} observed that tail-distribution degradation is most acute in the earliest generations, with minority modes vanishing before the output distribution stabilizes.
24	Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws demonstrating that tail probability mass is lost at rates predictable from model and data scale.
25	Our $\Kempirical = 2$ provides a complementary, classifier-based measurement of this phenomenon: the information-theoretic discrimination boundary is reached after just two generation steps.
26	Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} proved convergence to a fixed point for self-consuming generative models; $\Kempirical = 2$ indicates that, operationally, the approach to this fixed point is rapid enough that adjacent-generation distinctions collapse within two steps.
27	
28	Importantly, $\Kempirical = 2$ is an \emph{operational} lower bound conditioned on the 15-dimensional hand-crafted feature set; the \emph{theoretical} boundary $\Ktheory$ may be strictly higher.
29	Preliminary evidence from a neural probing experiment supports this distinction.
30	A frozen Qwen2.5-1.5B encoder (1536-dimensional last-layer representations) paired with a lightweight MLP classifier (Table~\ref{tab:s7_neural_probe}) achieves 2v3 $\auc = 0.6195$ ($\text{std} = 0.0094$) on the Qwen-continuation dataset, exceeding the $\theta = 0.60$ threshold that the same dataset's LightGBM classifier fails to cross ($\auc = 0.5609$; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}).
31	This yields $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$: the learned representation recovers one additional discriminable boundary that the hand-crafted features miss.
32	The improvement is concentrated at the 2v3 pair ($+$5.86\,pp over LightGBM); at the already-separable 1v2 boundary the neural probe achieves 0.6983 versus 0.6112, a substantial gain but one that does not alter the boundary determination.
33	At 3v4, the neural probe reaches $\auc = 0.5930$---below $\theta$ but closer to the threshold than any hand-crafted configuration---suggesting that a still richer representation might push the boundary further.
34	The lossy-channel narrative remains intact: even with 1536-dimensional frozen representations, the discrimination boundary extends to only three steps, confirming that the information bottleneck of recursive generation is shallow even with substantially richer representations.
35	These results are preliminary: they cover a single model-dataset pair (Qwen-continuation) and lack bootstrap confidence intervals; cross-model validation on Pythia and OLMo is pending.
36	
37	The invariance of $\Kempirical = 2$ across decoding strategies merits emphasis.
38	Greedy decoding, nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.9$), $T{=}0.7$, and $T{=}1.2$ all yield $\Kempirical = 2$ (Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay}; Table~\ref{tab:s2_decoding}), with 1v2 $\auc$ spanning a narrow range of [0.6866, 0.7039].
39	Higher decoding entropy modestly increases signal strength ($\auc_{1,2}$: 0.69 greedy $\to$ 0.70 at $T{=}1.2$) but does not shift the boundary.
40	This robustness suggests that $\Kempirical$ is governed by the fundamental information bottleneck of the generation process rather than by surface-level properties of the sampling algorithm.
41	
42	\subsection{Implications of Cross-Model Transfer}
43	\label{sec:discuss_transfer}
44	
45	The cross-model transfer results (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}) indicate that depth signals are largely encoded in text-level statistical properties rather than generator-specific artifacts.
46	Classifiers trained on Pythia-1.4B and evaluated on OLMo-1B retain 90--92\% of within-model accuracy, and the broader continuation-mode transfer matrix shows 80--92\% retention across all model pairs (Table~\ref{tab:transfer_matrix}; see Table~\ref{tab:s1_transfer} for the full matrix).
47	At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model $\auc$ exceeds 0.96 across all tested model pairs, confirming that binary contamination detection is fully transferable across the tested generators.
48	
49	The practical implication is direct: a single depth classifier trained on one model's outputs can be deployed to estimate generational depth for texts produced by other models, without model-specific retraining.
50	This transferability extends the utility of depth estimation to open-web settings where the generating model is unknown---precisely the scenario where depth-aware data curation is most needed.
51	
52	Two caveats bound this conclusion.
53	First, the text-intrinsic component dominates, as evidenced by high cross-model transfer retention (80--92\% across continuation-mode pairs), yet a nontrivial model-specific residual persists.
54	The Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo pair, which spans different architectures and training corpora, achieves the highest cross-family retention (90--92\%), consistent with the depth signal being largely architecture-agnostic within continuation mode.
55	Second, Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$OLMo retention (80--85\%) is lower than Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (90--92\%), indicating that model family similarity modulates transfer even among continuation-mode configurations.
56	
57	\subsection{Feature Importance Across Decoding Strategies}
58	\label{sec:discuss_features}
59	
60	While $\Kempirical = 2$ is invariant to decoding strategy (4/4 configurations), the feature importance ordering is not uniformly consistent.
61	Greedy decoding and $T{=}0.7$ share highly correlated feature rankings (Spearman $\rho = 0.914$), with top features dominated by vocabulary diversity measures: \texttt{self\_bleu}, \texttt{hapax\_ratio}, and \texttt{ttr}.
62	In contrast, greedy versus $T{=}1.2$ yields a lower correlation ($\rho = 0.53$, $p = 0.041$; suggestive but nonsignificant after Bonferroni correction for 6 pairwise comparisons), with $T{=}1.2$ promoting \texttt{hapax\_ratio}, \texttt{ttr}, and \texttt{surp\_skew} to the top ranks.
63	Notably, \texttt{freq\_entropy} rises from rank~10 under greedy ($\auc = 0.5139$) to rank~5 under $T{=}1.2$ ($\auc = 0.5905$), illustrating how high-entropy decoding amplifies frequency-distribution artifacts.
64	
65	This dissociation reveals an important distinction: the \emph{existence} of the depth boundary is robust, but the \emph{optimal feature subset} for detecting it depends on the sampling strategy.
66	High-entropy decoding amplifies frequency-distribution artifacts while attenuating vocabulary-diversity signals, shifting which text properties carry the most discriminative power without altering whether adjacent generations can be distinguished.
67	For practitioners, this implies that a universal depth classifier should incorporate features from multiple groups---surprisal moments, vocabulary diversity, and frequency tail statistics---to maintain performance across unknown decoding conditions.
68	
69	The cross-model feature ordering (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}) provides a complementary perspective: among continuation-mode models, single-feature $\auc$ rankings are highly consistent (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$), with surprisal-variance features---\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std}, \texttt{surp\_d2\_std}---dominating uniformly.
70	A genuine limitation, however, is that depth-pair-level agreement weakens to $\tau \approx 0.37$ at the 1v2 boundary (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}), indicating that the relative contribution of individual features at the discrimination boundary varies across models even when the aggregate ordering is shared.
71	
72	\subsection{LLM Zero-Shot Baseline}
73	\label{sec:discuss_llm}
74	
75	Frontier LLMs provide a natural baseline for depth estimation.
76	On a 500-sample test set with 5 depth classes (depths 0--4), excluding depth~5 from the 6-class range used in the main feature-based experiments since depths $\geq 3$ are mutually indistinguishable ($\Kempirical = 2$), GPT-5.5 achieves 33.2\% accuracy (MAE = 1.10) and Claude Opus~4.6 achieves 33.1\% accuracy (MAE = 1.15)---both below the OBD-LightGBM baseline of 38.6\% (MAE = 1.11; see Table~\ref{tab:s3_llm_zeroshot} for per-depth confusion matrices).
77	Simultaneously, both models achieve approximately 88\% binary accuracy on the human-vs.-synthetic distinction (GPT-5.5: 87.8\%, Claude: 88.2\%).
78	
79	This gap between binary detection and depth estimation is informative.
80	Frontier LLMs can reliably determine \emph{whether} a text is machine-generated but cannot estimate \emph{how many generations of recursive processing} it has undergone.
81	Depth estimation requires sensitivity to subtle distributional shifts between adjacent generations---shifts orders of magnitude smaller than the human-vs.-machine gap.
82	The 15-dimensional statistical feature pipeline, despite its simplicity, captures these fine-grained shifts more effectively than frontier LLMs in a zero-shot setting.
83	This motivates the dedicated feature-engineering approach: the task demands specialized statistical sensitivity rather than general language understanding.
84	We evaluate only zero-shot prompting; few-shot or chain-of-thought strategies may narrow the gap and warrant future investigation.
85	
86	\subsection{Limitations}
87	\label{sec:limitations}
88	
89	We identify seven limitations that bound the generalizability of our findings.
90	
91	\emph{Model scale.}
92	All experiments use models at or below 1.5B parameters (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct).
93	Larger models may produce higher-fidelity text with weaker depth signatures, potentially shifting $\Kempirical$ beyond~2.
94	
95	\emph{Prompt-chain versus retrain-chain.}
96	Our recursive generation protocol is a prompt-chain: the same fixed model repeatedly generates from the previous output.
97	Real-world model collapse involves retrain-chains, where models are retrained on data from earlier generations~\cite{shumailov2024collapse}.
98	Retrain-chains introduce additional degradation through training dynamics, potentially producing different $\Kstar$ values.
99	
100	\emph{Language and domain.}
101	All experiments use English text from the C4 corpus.
102	Depth dynamics may differ across languages, domains (e.g., code, scientific text), and source corpora with different distributional properties.
103	
104	\emph{Decoding coverage.}
105	We test four decoding strategies (greedy, nucleus $p{=}0.9$, $T{=}0.7$, $T{=}1.2$).
106	Other strategies---top-$k$ sampling, beam search, contrastive decoding---remain untested and may yield different feature importance patterns or boundary behavior.
107	
108	\emph{Threshold sensitivity.}
109	$\Kempirical$ depends on the operational threshold $\theta$.
110	$\Kempirical \geq 2$ across $\theta \in \{0.55, 0.60, 0.65\}$ for all four decoding strategies, rising to $\Kempirical = 3$ at $\theta = 0.55$ (all four 2v3 $\auc$ values exceed 0.55) and returning to $\Kempirical = 2$ at $\theta \in \{0.60, 0.65\}$.
111	At $\theta = 0.70$, three of four decoding configurations collapse to $\Kempirical = 1$; only the high-temperature setting ($T{=}1.2$) retains $\Kempirical = 2$, consistent with its elevated 1v2 $\auc$ (0.7039).
112	Beyond decoding parameters, the threshold sensitivity extends to generation mode: at $\theta{=}0.70$, $\Kempirical{=}1$ for all four model-mode configurations; at $\theta{=}0.65$, continuation-mode configurations already drop to $\Kempirical{=}1$, while rewrite mode retains $\Kempirical{=}2$.
113	Our current analysis primarily covers the decoding configuration axis.
114	The boundary is robust within a practical range but not invariant to threshold choice; our conclusions are conditioned on $\theta = 0.60$.
115	
116	\emph{Boundary marginality.}
117	The $\Kempirical = 2$ determination is statistically significant but numerically marginal at both ends.
118	On the lower side, Qwen-continuation's 1v2 CI lower bound (0.6015) exceeds $\theta = 0.60$ by only $+$0.15\,pp.
119	On the upper side, Qwen-rewrite's 2v3 CI upper bound (0.5991) falls below $\theta$ by only $-$0.09\,pp.
120	This narrow margin means that small changes in the feature set or classifier could shift the boundary---as the neural probe results confirm, where a richer representation pushes the 2v3 pair above $\theta$ on the Qwen-continuation dataset (Section~\ref{sec:discuss_kstar}).
121	Importantly, all eight boundary comparisons (four 1v2 and four 2v3) yield permutation $p < 0.01$, confirming that the statistical significance of the distinction is not in doubt---only its proximity to the operational threshold.
122	
123	\emph{Operational versus theoretical boundary.}
124	$\Kempirical$ is an operational lower bound that depends on the specific feature set and classifier.
125	$\Ktheory$ may be strictly greater; a more expressive classifier or richer feature representation could push $\Kempirical$ higher.
126	Preliminary neural probing results provide direct evidence for this gap: on the Qwen-continuation dataset, a frozen-encoder MLP achieves $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$ (2v3 $\auc = 0.6195$) compared to $\Kempirical = 2$ with 15-dimensional hand-crafted features (2v3 $\auc = 0.5609$; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}).
127	This confirms that the 15D feature set does not saturate the available depth signal and that $\Ktheory \geq 3$.
128	However, the neural probe result rests on a single dataset and awaits cross-model validation and bootstrap confidence intervals before a firm revision of the headline $\Kempirical$ can be claimed.
129	
130	\emph{Feature representation.}
131	The 15-dimensional hand-crafted feature set, while interpretable and transferable, is not optimal.
132	A preliminary neural probing experiment demonstrates that frozen LLM embeddings (1536 dimensions) paired with a lightweight MLP push $\Kempirical$ from~2 to~3 on the Qwen-continuation dataset (Section~\ref{sec:discuss_kstar}), confirming that learned representations capture depth-discriminative patterns that statistical features miss.
133	The magnitude of the gain---2v3 $\auc$ rising from 0.5609 to 0.6195---indicates meaningful recoverable signal beyond what hand-crafted features extract.
134	Full characterization of this gap, including cross-model generalization and bootstrap uncertainty quantification, remains future work.
135	
136	\paragraph{Graduated Filtering.}
137	Results for graduated filtering will be added upon completion of ongoing experiments.
138	
139	\subsection{Broader Impact}
140	\label{sec:broader_impact}
141	
142	The $\Kempirical = 2$ boundary has implications beyond the immediate scope of depth classification.
143	
144	\paragraph{Synthetic data curation.}
145	The practical consequence of $\Kempirical = 2$ is a three-tier taxonomy of text quality: human-authored (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$).
146	Texts at depth~$\geq 2$ are mutually indistinguishable and can be treated as a single category for curation purposes.
147	For practitioners filtering training data, this implies that a single round of synthetic rewriting suffices to make text statistically indistinguishable from text that has undergone multiple rounds of recycling---a form of one-wash laundering that limits the granularity of quality-based filtering.
148	This underscores the urgency of deploying depth-aware curation mechanisms before the first generation step, rather than relying on post-hoc detection.
149	Graduated filtering strategies that exploit this trichotomy may outperform binary human/synthetic filters, as the coarse ordinal signal (human / shallow / deep) captures the dominant axis of quality variation.
150	
151	\paragraph{Relation to model collapse.}
152	Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} and Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} study model collapse under \emph{retrain-chains}, where models are iteratively trained on their own outputs.
153	Our prompt-chain protocol measures an adjacent but distinct phenomenon: the degradation of statistical distinguishability under recursive generation by a fixed model.
154	The rapid convergence we observe ($\Kempirical = 2$) is consistent with the theoretical prediction of convergence to a fixed point, but the precise relationship between prompt-chain $\Kempirical$ and retrain-chain convergence rates remains an open question.
155	If prompt-chain depth signals serve as an observable proxy for early-stage model collapse, depth estimation could provide a lightweight diagnostic for data curation pipelines without requiring expensive retraining experiments.
156	
157	\paragraph{AI text detection.}
158	Current AI text detection is predominantly binary: human versus machine.
159	Our results suggest that \emph{depth-aware} detection provides a strictly more informative signal.
160	The near-perfect 0v1 separability ($\auc > 0.99$) confirms that binary detection is reliable at this scale, but the 1v2 boundary ($\auc$: 0.61--0.70) reveals that first-generation text retains measurable statistical distance from deeper synthetic text.
161	This additional dimension---how many generations of processing a text has undergone---may prove valuable for provenance tracking and corpus quality assessment, where the binary human/AI label elides important distinctions between lightly and heavily recycled content.
